exercises.title: Partition, then recurse
exercises.task: Here is Hoare's idea as Go code. Before pressing Run, answer the question in the lesson: random input or sorted input, which one is faster with the last element as pivot? Then run it and look at the comparison counts, especially the second line. The third line is the same sorted input with a random pivot.

exercises.title: Write partition
exercises.task: Your turn to write partition, the version from the trace in the lesson. The pivot is the last element. Walk the range with j, and keep the promise: everything before i is smaller than the pivot. At the end, the pivot goes to i, and that is the index you return.
hints: i marks the end of the "smaller than the pivot" part: it starts at lo.
For each j from lo to hi-1: if a[j] < pivot, swap a[i] and a[j], then i++.
At the end swap a[i] and a[hi] (the pivot) and return i.

exercises.title: A percentile without sorting
exercises.task: You want the median of 100 000 values, not a sorted list of them. Hoare's FIND: partition, see where the pivot landed, and continue only in the side that contains position k. Write Select. It must compare only through less, because the check counts the calls: it must stay far below what a full sort needs. And the check also gives it sorted input: remember the trap.
hints: Partition as in e2, but compare with less(a[j], pivot). If the pivot lands at k, done; if k is before it, continue left; otherwise right. A loop, not two recursive calls.
Pick a random pivot (swap a random element of the range to the end first, with rand.Intn): with the last element, sorted input costs n²/2 comparisons, and the check tries sorted input.
Work on a copy (slices.Clone): Select must not reorder the caller's slice.
